summary.text: For every \(t\ge0\), set \(n=2^{t+3}+1\); Legendre’s binary digit-sum formula for factorial valuations, together with the fact that removing primes from these intervals does not change their \(2\)-adic valuation, gives \(v_2(a(n-1))=2^{t+3}+t+1\) and \(v_2(a(n))=2^{t+3}-1\). Thus \(a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\) for each of these infinitely many distinct \(n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
T_n=\frac{n(n+1)}2.
\]
Thus the sequence is
\[
a(n)=\prod_{\substack{T_{n-1}<k\le T_n\\ k\text{ composite}}}k.
\]
We will exhibit infinitely many indices \(n>1\) for which \(a(n-1)\nmid a(n)\). The indices will be
\[
n_t=2^{t+3}+1,\qquad t=0,1,2,\ldots.
\]

For a positive integer \(m\), write \(v_2(m)\) for the exponent of \(2\) in its prime factorization, and write \(s_2(m)\) for the sum of the binary digits of \(m\), equivalently the number of ones in its base-two expansion. We use the standard binary form of Legendre’s formula:
\[
v_2(m!)=m-s_2(m).
\]
For completeness, Legendre’s formula first gives
\[
v_2(m!)=\sum_{j\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{m}{2^j}\right\rfloor.
\]
If \(m=\sum_i \varepsilon_i2^i\), with each \(\varepsilon_i\in\{0,1\}\), then
\[
\sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac m{2^j}\right\rfloor
 =\sum_i\varepsilon_i(2^i-1)
 =m-\sum_i\varepsilon_i
 =m-s_2(m),
\]
which proves the stated form.

Fix an arbitrary integer \(t\ge0\), and put
\[
q=2^{t+3},\qquad p=2^{t+2}=\frac q2.
\]
We compare \(a(q)\) and \(a(q+1)\). Define the three consecutive triangular endpoints
\[
C=T_{q-1}=\binom q2,
\qquad
A=T_q=\binom{q+1}2,
\qquad
B=T_{q+1}=\binom{q+2}2.
\]
Since \(q=2p\), these endpoints have the useful forms
\[
C=\frac{q(q-1)}2=p(q-1),
\]
\[
A=\frac{q(q+1)}2=p(q+1),
\]
and
\[
B=\frac{(q+1)(q+2)}2=(q+1)(p+1).
\]
They also satisfy
\[
A-C=q,
\qquad
B-A=q+1.
\]
Consequently the block defining \(a(q)\) is
\[
C+1,C+2,\ldots,A,
\]
a block of \(q\) consecutive integers, while the block defining \(a(q+1)\) is
\[
A+1,A+2,\ldots,B,
\]
a block of \(q+1\) consecutive integers.

We next explain why, for the purpose of computing the exponent of \(2\), we may ignore the restriction that only composite numbers are included. Since \(q\ge8\), we have
\[
C+1=\binom q2+1>2.
\]
Thus every integer occurring in either of the two blocks is greater than \(2\). Every even integer greater than \(2\) is composite. It follows that every number omitted from either block-product because it is prime is odd, and hence contributes zero to the \(2\)-adic valuation. Therefore
\[
v_2(a(q))=v_2\left(\prod_{k=C+1}^{A}k\right)

a nd
\]
\[
v_2(a(q+1))=v_2\left(\prod_{k=A+1}^{B}k\right).
\]
In other words, filtering out the primes does not change either \(2\)-adic valuation.

We now compute the first valuation. Because
\[
\prod_{k=C+1}^{A}k=\frac{A!}{C!},
\]
additivity of \(v_2\) gives
\[
v_2(a(q))=v_2(A!)-v_2(C!).
\]
Using the binary form of Legendre’s formula,
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2(a(q))
&=(A-s_2(A))-(C-s_2(C))\\
&=(A-C)+s_2(C)-s_2(A)\\
&=q+s_2(C)-s_2(A).
\end{aligned}
\]
It remains to compute the two binary digit sums.

First,
\[
C=p(q-1)=2^{t+2}(2^{t+3}-1).
\]
The number \(2^{t+3}-1\) has exactly \(t+3\) ones in binary:
\[
2^{t+3}-1=(11\cdots1)_2,
\]
with ones in positions \(0,1,\ldots,t+2\). Multiplication by \(2^{t+2}\) merely shifts the binary expansion and does not alter the number of ones. Hence
\[
s_2(C)=t+3.
\]
Second,
\[
A=p(q+1)=2^{t+2}(1+2^{t+3}).
\]
The factor \(1+2^{t+3}\) has exactly two ones in binary, and again multiplication by a power of two only shifts the digits. Therefore
\[
s_2(A)=2.
\]
Substitution yields
\[
\boxed{v_2(a(q))=q+(t+3)-2=q+t+1.}
\]

We similarly compute the valuation of the next term. Since
\[
\prod_{k=A+1}^{B}k=\frac{B!}{A!},
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_2(a(q+1))
&=v_2(B!)-v_2(A!)\\
&=(B-s_2(B))-(A-s_2(A))\\
&=(B-A)+s_2(A)-s_2(B)\\
&=(q+1)+s_2(A)-s_2(B).
\end{aligned}
\]
We already know that \(s_2(A)=2\). To calculate \(s_2(B)\), expand
\[
B=(q+1)(p+1)=1+p+q+pq.
\]
In terms of powers of two this is
\[
B=2^0+2^{t+2}+2^{t+3}+2^{2t+5}.
\]
The exponents are strictly increasing:
\[
0<t+2<t+3<2t+5
\]
for every \(t\ge0\). Thus no carrying occurs in this sum, and the binary expansion of \(B\) has exactly four ones. Hence
\[
s_2(B)=4.
\]
It follows that
\[
\boxed{v_2(a(q+1))=(q+1)+2-4=q-1.}
\]

Comparing the two exact valuations gives
\[
v_2(a(q))-v_2(a(q+1))
=(q+t+1)-(q-1)=t+2>0.
\]
Thus \(a(q)\) contains a strictly higher power of \(2\) than \(a(q+1)\). If \(a(q)\) divided \(a(q+1)\), then the exponent of every prime in \(a(q)\) would be at most its exponent in \(a(q+1)\), in particular
\[
v_2(a(q))\le v_2(a(q+1)).
\]
The strict reverse inequality proves that
\[
a(q)\nmid a(q+1).
\]
Since \(q=2^{t+3}\), this says that for every \(t\ge0\),
\[
a\bigl((2^{t+3}+1)-1\bigr)\nmid a(2^{t+3}+1).
\]
Moreover, every index \(n_t=2^{t+3}+1\) is greater than \(1\). The indices are all distinct—in fact they are strictly increasing with \(t\)—so they form an infinite set. Therefore there are infinitely many integers \(n>1\) for which
\[
a(n-1)\nmid a(n).
\]
This disproves the conjecture that only finitely many such integers exist.
